clue.text: Put wise uncle with Independent cryptic

indicators.note: something cryptic is obscure and disguised, so the letters are scrambled out of their plain order

parts.note: taken as written
I is the standard abbreviation for Independent

explanation.surface: A worldly uncle teams up with the Independent newspaper's cryptic crossword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Independent cryptic' reads as a newspaper puzzle, but 'cryptic' is the scrambling signal working on the uncle plus I.
explanation.definitionFit: To clue someone in is to inform them, and putting someone wise means telling them what is going on.

clue.text: Fine tyres, as he periodically offers

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so only every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: A tyre salesman periodically offers fine tyres.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the comma and the gaps: the even letters of the run of words spell the answer, and 'offers' just links it to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: As a casual reply, the slang affirmative and 'fine' both signal agreement or acceptance.

clue.text: Escalating argument about low roof, taking away nothing from brewery facilities

indicators.note: in a down clue, escalating means climbing upward, so the letters read from bottom to top
about means around, so one piece is wrapped around the others

parts.note: a spat is a petty quarrel
to low is to make a cow's noise

indicators.note: to take away is to subtract, so some letters are removed from a word

parts.note: taken as written, before letters are removed
O looks like zero, nothing; this letter is removed
of can mean from, as in 'a man of Kent'; these letters are removed

explanation.surface: A heated dispute over a low ceiling in a brewery's bar.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'nothing' (O) and 'from' (OF) are taken out of ROOF, leaving R. SPAT then goes about MOO plus R, and the whole is read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A taproom is a bar where beer is served from the tap, often attached to a brewery as its drinking room.

clue.text: Time abandons opposition to US attention-seeker

indicators.note: when something abandons a place it leaves, so that letter goes missing

parts.note: 'us and them' are opposing sides
T is the abbreviation for time; it is removed

explanation.surface: Time runs out on resistance to an American publicity-seeker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'US' looks like America but is the pronoun 'us', whose opposite in 'us and them' is 'them'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hem is a little cough or throat-clearing, a short form of 'ahem', made to attract someone's notice.

clue.text: Old serfs, all bar leader on the line

indicators.note: bar means except, so the word is taken without its first letter

parts.note: all is THE LOT, here minus its first letter
RY is the abbreviation for railway, a line

explanation.surface: Old serfs, all except their chief, are lined up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All' is THE LOT, which loses its T; 'on' places it before the railway line in an across-or-down build.
explanation.definitionFit: Helots were the state-owned serfs of ancient Sparta, and the collective noun covers that whole class of bondsmen.

clue.text: Gum spasm beyond old lady's control?

parts.note: MA is an old lady, a mother; with the possessive S
a tic is an involuntary twitch
surface padding: a twitch is by nature beyond anyone's control

explanation.surface: A twitch of the gums that the old lady cannot control.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally the second half places the twitch beyond, after, the mother's possessive: the tic belongs to Ma.
explanation.definitionFit: Mastic is an aromatic resin from a Mediterranean tree, used as chewing material and varnish.

clue.text: No way sorry in business after completely hiking figure

indicators.note: in a down clue, hiking lifts everything upward, so the whole string reads bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
RD is the abbreviation for road
'eh?' asks for repetition like 'sorry?'
at and in both mean located there
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: A hiker apologises for refusing a route through business.
explanation.walkthrough: Five short pieces join in clue order, then the whole chain is turned upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: An octahedron is a solid geometric figure with eight flat faces, such as two square pyramids base to base.

clue.text: A stack o' Edinburgh's premier bakes

definitions.text: A stack o' Edinburgh's premier bakes

indicators.note: baking transforms raw ingredients, so the letters are mixed and reshaped

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: premier means first, so only the opening letter is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of the city

explanation.surface: A pile of the finest baked goods from Edinburgh.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the jumbled letters make a pile of the Scottish capital's best-known baked biscuits.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatcakes are flat savoury biscuits of oatmeal, a Scottish staple, so a stack of them is Edinburgh's premier bake.

clue.text: Divert punchy type, sounding out Hornsey area?

parts.note: Muhammad Ali, the boxer

indicators.note: sounding something out means saying it, so the letters come from speech rather than spelling

parts.note: Hornsey's London postcode district is N8

explanation.surface: Distracting a boxer by reading out a north London address.
explanation.walkthrough: Hornsey is a district of north London with postcode N8; said aloud as 'en-eight' it gives the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate affections or property is to divert or transfer them elsewhere, a legal and literary sense.

clue.text: With change of heart, it's possible for cunning to function in Opposition

indicators.note: a change of heart alters the centre, so the two middle letters are rearranged

parts.note: art is craft or guile
'can' says something is possible

explanation.surface: A politician's cunning works best when they sit in Opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart change swaps the middle pair of the joined word. 'Opposition' is not Parliament: the tangent is opposite over adjacent, and the inverse function works from that ratio.
explanation.definitionFit: Arctan is the inverse tangent, a trigonometric function giving the angle whose opposite-to-adjacent ratio is known.

clue.text: Carrier of hot liquid has overall covering bottom

indicators.note: to cover is to wrap around, so one piece goes on either side of another

parts.note: a net figure is the overall one after deductions
a vacuum flask keeps drinks hot

explanation.surface: Someone carrying a hot drink wears overalls over their behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overall' looks like a work garment but means net, and 'bottom' is an adjective, not a backside.
explanation.definitionFit: Nethermost means lowest of all, the furthest down, just as bottom does as an adjective.

clue.text: To which extent Curie elongated cells

parts.note: 'as' measures degree, as in 'as far as'
Ci is the symbol for the curie, a unit of radioactivity

explanation.surface: How far did Marie Curie stretch her cells?
explanation.walkthrough: Curie suggests the scientist, but the wordplay uses the unit named after her.
explanation.definitionFit: Asci are the sac-like spore-bearing structures of certain fungi, long narrow single cells in botany.

clue.text: Remove rights to run escort agency

indicators.note: remove means take away, so certain letters drop out of the words

parts.note: R and RT are both abbreviations for right; they are removed
taken as written; the letters left in place after the deletion are no hidden word, just a coincidence of the method

explanation.surface: Stripping an escort agency of its licence to operate.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different right abbreviations go: R from the first word, RT from the second. 'Escort agency' looks like one phrase, but the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: UNESCO is the United Nations' educational, scientific and cultural organisation, a specialised UN body.

clue.text: Rubber bullet's taken out sandwich ingredients!

indicators.note: taking something out removes it, so those letters vanish from the word

parts.note: taken as written
a BLT holds bacon, lettuce and tomato

explanation.surface: A rubber bullet has knocked out the fillings of a sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rubber bullet' is a false unit: Rubber is the definition. The three letters of a BLT are taken out of the bullet, scattered as they are.
explanation.definitionFit: Ule is a Central American tree whose latex yields rubber, so the tree itself is a rubber.

clue.text: For whom retail therapy is no therapy

definitions.text: For whom retail therapy is no therapy

parts.words: For whom retail therapy is no therapy
parts.note: surface reading: someone for whom treatment does not work
setter's reading: shopping to cheer up feeds an addiction instead of curing anything

explanation.walkthrough: Retail therapy is jokey slang for shopping to lift the mood; for a compulsive buyer it is the problem, not the cure.
explanation.definitionFit: A compulsive spender is addicted to buying, so a spree only deepens the habit rather than easing any distress.

clue.text: Looks over hatches again

definitions.meaning: second meaning: re-covers with a criss-cross pattern of lines

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hatches' suggests eggs or doors, but here it is cross-hatching, marking with criss-cross lines that form a chequered pattern.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both examining something a second time and marking a chequered pattern on it once more.

clue.text: Support particularly like a chocolate teapot?

parts.note: ESP is the abbreviation for especially
'of no use' is written O USE, nothing plus use

explanation.surface: Backing something that is as useful as a chocolate teapot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As much use as a chocolate teapot' is a British put-down for anything useless, since it would melt; no use becomes O plus USE.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a cause is to adopt and back it, so the verb matches support as a transitive verb.

clue.text: Columbo's employer perhaps beribboned hastily

indicators.note: something beribboned is wrapped in a ribbon, so one piece is bound inside another

parts.note: a sash is a broad ribbon worn across the body
Columbo was a Los Angeles Police Department detective

explanation.surface: The TV detective's force hurriedly decorated with ribbons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beribboned' does double work: it says the force is inside, and the ribbon itself is the sash.
explanation.definitionFit: Done slapdash means done carelessly and in a hurry, so as an adverb it matches hastily.

clue.text: Former authority assumed regressively by "Ma'am"/"Sir" as teachers

indicators.note: regressing means going backwards, so the letters run right to left
to assume is to take on, so the letters are taken up inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the forms of address

explanation.surface: Pupils addressing teachers as Ma'am or Sir is an old-fashioned kind of authority.
explanation.walkthrough: The punctuation hides the join: the last M of the first title, all of the second, then AS and the first T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsarism was autocratic rule by the Russian emperors, a system of government that ended in 1917.

clue.text: Mark takes Charlie for a spin in recce vehicle

indicators.note: taking something for a spin turns it round, and here it means taken out
to take in is to hold, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a scar is the mark of a healed wound
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
someone taken for a spin is out

explanation.surface: A man named Mark gives Charlie a ride in a reconnaissance vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Mark looks like a first name, but it is a scar; taking Charlie for a spin means taking C out, and that goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A scout car is a light armoured military vehicle used for reconnaissance, the work a recce does.

clue.text: CEO cages a cuckoo

indicators.note: to cage is to enclose, so one piece is shut inside another

parts.note: MD, managing director, is the chief executive
taken as written

explanation.surface: A company boss keeps a cuckoo in a cage.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird is the definition; MD is the usual British title for a company's chief executive.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuckoo is informal for crazy, so both words describe someone out of their mind.

clue.text: Rings of colour winding poetically over a ploughed lea

indicators.note: something winding twists about, so its letters do not keep their order
ploughing churns the soil, so these letters are churned into a new order

parts.note: o'er is the poetic contraction of over
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Coloured rings form as a stream winds poetically across a ploughed meadow.
explanation.walkthrough: Two signals cover the same pool of letters: the poet's o'er, A, and the meadow word, all mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: Areolae are small circles of differently coloured skin or tissue, such as the ring around a nipple.

clue.text: A bit of a buffet sadly knocked over poet on cycle

indicators.note: knocking something over upends it, so the letters run the other way
a cycle goes round, so a letter moves from one end to the other

parts.note: 'alas' is said sadly
a bard is a poet

explanation.surface: A poet riding a bicycle crashes into the buffet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' gives the exclamation of regret, and 'on cycle' moves the poet's final letter to the front; the definition is only one part of a buffet.
explanation.definitionFit: A salad bar is a counter of self-service salads, one section of a larger buffet spread.

clue.text: Conductors briefly try to earn money playing music pieces

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.words: try to earn money playing music
parts.note: to busk is to perform in the street for money, here cut short
chess pieces are men

explanation.surface: Orchestra conductors busking for small change with their musical pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conductors' and 'music' suggest an orchestra, but these are the ticket collectors on buses.
explanation.definitionFit: Bus conductors collected fares on board, and busmen is a collective term for bus crews.

clue.text: Elected bores given the go-ahead behaved swinishly

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into, so one piece goes into another

parts.note: OK'd, approved
a winning candidate is in

explanation.surface: Elected bores, once approved, acted like pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bores' looks like a noun for dull people, but it is a verb, drilling one piece into the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Pigs grunt, so making the grunting noise of a pig is behaving as a swine does, literally.

clue.text: Overwhelm mischief-maker carrying revolver butt-first?

indicators.note: to carry is to hold, so one piece goes inside another
a gun's butt is its back end, so the end letter is brought to the front

parts.note: elves are mischievous sprites
a revolver is a handgun

explanation.surface: Swamp a troublemaker who is carrying a gun held the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' hints at turning round, but the move is a rotation: the gun's last letter comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To engulf is to sweep over and swallow up completely, as water or fire overwhelms something.

clue.text: Tuber fled Docklands stops

indicators.note: a stop plugs a gap from inside, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the letters sit across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A potato fled from the stations of London's Docklands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stops' looks like railway stations; it is the signal that the words contain the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An eddo is the edible starchy corm of the taro plant, eaten like a potato in the tropics.

clue.text: What's left spaces on back for newly filled in scoreline?

definitions.text: What's left spaces on back for newly filled in scoreline?

indicators.note: going back means running the opposite way, so the letters read in reverse
freshly filled in means the old contents are swapped for new ones

parts.note: the first and last letters stay, the middle is replaced
port is the left side of a ship
gaps are spaces

explanation.surface: A newspaper's back page leaves blank spaces to be filled with late scores.
explanation.walkthrough: The scoreline keeps only its outer letters, and the naval left plus spaces turned around replace its middle. Read whole, the clue describes the newspaper section itself.
explanation.definitionFit: British papers traditionally print the sport on the back pages, with space held for the latest match results.

clue.text: Prude revelling in Grundyism, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: A prude takes delight in strict moral censure.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: Mrs Grundy is an old byword for priggish disapproval, from a 1798 play.
explanation.definitionFit: A prig is a self-righteously proper person who delights in the moral fault-finding Mrs Grundy stands for.

clue.text: Ignoring the odds, persist with this person's case

indicators.note: dropping the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

parts.note: second, fourth and sixth letters
this person, the speaker, has: I've

explanation.surface: Against the odds, someone keeps pursuing their legal case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This person's' is the setter's 'I has', written as I've; 'case' is grammar, not law.
explanation.definitionFit: The essive is a grammatical case, in Finnish for example, expressing a temporary state of being.

clue.text: Where sweet girl awaits husband in Calais, with all encompassing love

indicators.note: to encompass is to surround, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: taken as written
mari is French for husband
love is zero in tennis

explanation.surface: A sweet girl waits for her husband in Calais, with love all round.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition recalls the song '(Is This the Way to) Amarillo', where 'sweet Marie' waits; the French husband sits inside ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: Amarillo is the Texas city in Tony Christie's hit, the place where the singer's sweetheart Marie waits for him.

clue.text: Out of necessity, daughter called before wedding

indicators.note: out of means removed from, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: need is necessity
D is the abbreviation for daughter; it is removed

explanation.surface: A daughter phoned before the wedding because she had to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of necessity' reads as 'because it was needed', but it is the instruction to take D out.
explanation.definitionFit: Née, French for born, introduces a married woman's maiden name, the surname she had before marriage.
